title: Lechon sisig
intro: Leftover lechon or lechon kawali chopped small and fried until crackly, then tossed with onions, chilies, calamansi and a little lechon sauce. It is crunchy, tangy and savory, and it turns party leftovers into a new meal.

steps.text: Heat the oil in a wide, heavy pan over medium-high heat. Add the chopped lechon and fry, stirring only now and then, until the skin pieces turn crisp again and the fat renders.
Push the pork to one side, add the garlic and half the onions to the fat and cook until soft. Stir everything together.
Add the lechon sauce and soy sauce and stir-fry until the pork is glazed and sizzling.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the calamansi juice, chilies, pepper and the remaining onions.
If using the egg, crack it on top while the pan is still hot and stir it in at the table. Serve with calamansi halves.

tips: The chopped skin goes soft in the fridge, but a hot pan and a little patience bring the crunch back. Do not cover the pan or it will steam.

title: Chicken sisig
intro: Chicken thighs with their skin, seared until crisp, chopped with chicken livers and tossed with onions, chilies and calamansi. It has the tang and crunch of pork sisig in about an hour.

items.name: calamansi juice
items.note: for the marinade, plus 3 tbsp to finish

steps.text: Toss the chicken with 3 tablespoons calamansi juice, the soy sauce and half the garlic. Leave to marinate.
Heat the oil in a heavy pan over medium heat. Lay the chicken skin side down and cook until the skin is deep golden and crisp, then turn and cook through.
Fry the livers in the same pan until just cooked, about 4 minutes. Let everything rest a few minutes.
Chop the chicken and livers into small pieces.
Return the pan to medium-high heat with the drippings. Saute the remaining garlic and half the onions, then add the chopped chicken and stir-fry until the skin bits crisp up.
Off the heat, stir in the remaining calamansi juice, the chilies, pepper, the rest of the onions and the mayonnaise if using. Season with salt.
Top with a fried or raw egg if you like and serve hot.

tips: Thighs stay juicy and the skin is what makes it crunchy; breast meat comes out dry. Serve on a sizzling plate if you have one.

title: Tuna sisig
intro: Fresh tuna seared, diced and stir-fried with onions, chilies, soy sauce and calamansi, finished with a creamy touch of mayonnaise. It is meaty, tangy and quick, a good weeknight sisig.

steps.text: Season the tuna with 1 tablespoon calamansi juice, the salt and pepper and leave it while you chop the vegetables.
Heat 1 tablespoon of the oil in a pan over high heat. Sear the tuna until browned outside and just cooked through, about 3 minutes per side.
Let the tuna cool slightly, then cut it into small dice.
Heat the remaining oil and the butter over medium heat. Saute the garlic and half the onions until soft.
Add the tuna and soy sauce and stir-fry gently until the edges start to brown.
Off the heat, fold in the remaining calamansi juice, chilies, mayonnaise and the rest of the onions. Top with an egg if you like and serve with calamansi halves.

tips: Do not chop the tuna too fine or it turns mushy. Leftover grilled tuna jaw (panga) picked off the bone makes very good sisig too.

title: Bangus sisig
intro: Boneless milkfish fried until crisp, flaked and stir-fried with onions, chilies, soy sauce and calamansi. The crisp skin gives it crunch, and the belly fat keeps it rich and moist.

steps.text: Pat the bangus dry and rub both sides with the salt.
Heat the oil in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the fish skin side down first, then turn, until both sides are golden and crisp.
Drain on paper towels and let cool a little. Flake the fish into small pieces, keeping the crisp skin, and pick out any stray bones.
Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of oil. Saute the garlic, ginger and half the onions over medium heat until soft.
Add the flaked fish and soy sauce and stir-fry until the bits are crisp at the edges.
Off the heat, stir in the calamansi juice, chilies, pepper, the rest of the onions and the mayonnaise if using. Serve hot with rice.

tips: Leftover fried or grilled bangus works just as well; skip the frying and start at the saute.

title: Sisig na pusit
intro: Squid grilled or seared over high heat, chopped and tossed with onions, chilies, calamansi and a little butter. It is smoky, tender and tangy, with a pleasant chew.

steps.text: Pat the squid very dry and season with the salt.
Grill over hot charcoal or sear in a very hot pan with a little oil until lightly charred and just opaque, about 2 minutes per side.
Chop the squid into small pieces.
Heat the remaining oil and the butter in a pan over medium-high heat. Saute the garlic and half the onions until soft.
Add the squid and soy sauce and toss for 1 minute only, so the squid stays tender.
Off the heat, stir in the calamansi juice, chilies, pepper, remaining onions and the mayonnaise if using. Serve right away.

tips: Squid is tender when cooked very briefly or for a long time, and rubbery in between. Keep it fast here and have everything chopped before you start.

title: Tofu sisig
intro: Firm tofu cut small and fried until crisp, then tossed with onions, chilies, soy sauce, calamansi and a creamy mayonnaise dressing. It is crunchy outside, soft inside, and full of the familiar sisig tang.

steps.text: Wrap the tofu in a clean towel and press it under a heavy pan to remove water before cubing.
Heat the oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the tofu in batches, turning, until golden and crisp on all sides. Drain on paper towels.
Pour off all but 1 tablespoon of oil. Saute the garlic and half the onions until soft.
Return the tofu, add the soy sauce and toss over high heat until glazed.
Off the heat, stir in the calamansi juice, chilies, pepper, mayonnaise and the rest of the onions. Top with a fried egg if you like and serve hot.

tips: Pressing the tofu well is what makes it crisp; wet tofu spatters and stays soft. Toss in the dressing at the last minute so the crust holds.

title: Mushroom sisig
intro: Oyster mushrooms seared until browned and chewy, then chopped and tossed with onions, chilies, soy sauce and calamansi. It is savory, tangy and has a meaty bite without any meat.

steps.text: Heat 2 tablespoons of the oil in a wide pan over high heat. Add half the mushrooms in a single layer and leave them until browned underneath, then stir and cook until most of their liquid has evaporated. Repeat with the rest.
Chop the browned mushrooms roughly into small pieces.
Heat the remaining oil and the butter over medium heat. Saute the garlic and half the onions until soft.
Add the mushrooms and soy sauce and stir-fry until the edges turn crisp.
Off the heat, stir in the calamansi juice, chilies, pepper, the rest of the onions and the mayonnaise if using. Serve hot with rice.

tips: Oyster mushrooms give the chewiest, most meat-like bite; shiitake or button mushrooms also work. Do not crowd the pan: mushrooms that steam turn soft and gray instead of browning. Salt them only at the end.

title: Kinilaw na tanigue
intro: Cubes of very fresh Spanish mackerel cured in coconut vinegar with ginger, red onion and chilies. It is cold, sharp and clean-tasting, with firm, silky fish.

items.name: very fresh tanigue (Spanish mackerel) fillet
items.note: skin and dark flesh removed, cut into 3/4-inch cubes

steps.text: Use fish bought the same day, firm, with a clean sea smell. Keep it cold the whole time: chill the cubes in a glass or ceramic bowl set over ice.
Pour the rinsing vinegar over the fish, toss gently, then drain and discard the vinegar. This firms and cleans the surface.
Add the curing vinegar, calamansi juice, ginger, onion, chilies, salt and pepper. Toss gently.
Leave in the fridge, tossing once, until the outside of the cubes turns opaque white and the center is still slightly translucent.
Taste, adjust the salt and serve cold right away.

tips: Kinilaw is best within the hour; after that the fish keeps curing and turns chalky. Cut the fish with a sharp knife so the edges stay clean.

title: Kinilaw na tuna sa gata
intro: Fresh tuna cured briefly in vinegar, then finished with thick coconut cream, ginger, cucumber and chilies. The coconut softens the sourness and makes it rich, cool and creamy.

steps.text: Use tuna bought the same day from a fishmonger you trust, deep red and firm, and keep it on ice while you work.
Put the tuna in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl with the vinegar, ginger, onion and salt. Toss gently and refrigerate until the surface turns pale.
Pour off about half of the vinegar.
Stir in the coconut cream, cucumber and chilies. Taste and adjust the salt.
Chill briefly and serve cold the same day.

tips: Fresh coconut cream squeezed from grated coconut tastes best, but good canned coconut cream works. Add it only after the vinegar cure, or it will curdle.

title: Kinilaw na malasugi
intro: Cubes of fresh swordfish cured in calamansi and vinegar with tomato, red onion and ginger. It is bright, citrusy and juicy, with dense, meaty fish.

items.name: very fresh malasugi (swordfish) steak
items.note: skin and dark flesh removed, cut into 3/4-inch cubes

steps.text: Choose fish bought the same day, with firm, glossy flesh and no fishy smell. Keep it cold in a bowl set over ice.
Toss the cubes with the calamansi juice, vinegar, ginger and salt in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl.
Refrigerate, tossing once, until the fish is opaque on the outside and just translucent in the middle.
Fold in the tomatoes, onion, chilies and pepper. Taste and adjust the salt, then serve cold.

tips: Add the tomatoes at the end so they stay firm and do not water down the cure. Serve within the hour.

title: Kinilaw na tilapia
intro: Strips of very fresh tilapia cured in vinegar until white and firm, then mixed with ginger, onion, chilies and calamansi. It is mild, sour and refreshing, a budget kinilaw that uses an everyday fish.

items.name: large very fresh tilapia
items.note: about 1 kg total, filleted and skinned

steps.text: Use tilapia bought live or killed that morning, and fillet it yourself so you know it is fresh. Keep the fillets cold.
Cut the fillets into thin strips about 1/2 inch wide and remove any pin bones.
Put the fish in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl with the vinegar and salt. Toss and refrigerate, tossing now and then, until the fish is white all the way through.
Pour off about half of the vinegar. Add the calamansi juice, ginger, onion, chilies and pepper and toss.
Taste, adjust the salt and serve cold.

tips: Freshwater fish benefits from a fuller cure, so give tilapia longer in the vinegar than sea fish. Cutting thin strips helps the vinegar reach the center.

title: Kinilaw na hipon
intro: Peeled raw shrimp cured in calamansi and vinegar until pink and firm, tossed with cucumber, ginger, onion and chilies. It is sweet, sour and crisp, and best served very cold.

steps.text: Use shrimp bought alive or the same day, with firm, translucent flesh and no smell of ammonia. Keep them on ice.
Put the shrimp in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl with the calamansi juice, vinegar, ginger and salt. Toss well.
Refrigerate, tossing every 10 minutes, until the shrimp turn pink and opaque all the way through.
Drain off about half of the liquid. Fold in the cucumber, onion and chilies, taste for salt and serve cold.

tips: Halving the shrimp lengthwise lets the cure reach the center evenly. If any piece is still gray inside after 30 minutes, give it another 10.

title: Sinuglaw
intro: Smoky grilled pork belly mixed with fresh tuna kinilaw, cucumber, ginger and chilies. The warm, fatty pork and the cold, sour fish balance each other, making it a favorite with drinks or rice.

steps.text: Mix the pork with the soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic and pepper and leave to marinate.
Grill the pork over medium-hot charcoal or in a grill pan, turning often, until cooked through and charred at the edges.
Let the pork rest, then cut it into bite-size pieces.
While the pork grills, put the very fresh, ice-cold tuna in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl with the vinegar, ginger and salt. Refrigerate until the outside turns opaque.
Add the calamansi juice, onion, cucumber and chilies to the fish and toss.
Fold in the warm pork just before serving. Taste for salt and serve right away.

tips: Mix the pork in at the last minute so the fish stays cold and the pork stays smoky. Use fish bought the same day.

title: Kinilaw na tahong
intro: Fresh mussels blanched just until they open, then dressed in vinegar with ginger, onion, chilies and calamansi. They stay plump and sweet, with a sharp, clean dressing.

steps.text: Discard any mussels with cracked shells or that stay open when tapped. Use mussels bought alive the same day.
Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. Add the mussels and cook just until the shells open, then drain right away. Discard any that stay closed.
Remove the mussels from their shells and let them cool to room temperature.
Toss the mussels with the vinegar, calamansi juice, ginger, onion, chilies, salt and pepper in a glass or ceramic bowl.
Refrigerate to let the flavors soak in, then serve cold.

tips: Pull the mussels the moment they open; longer cooking shrinks and toughens them. Eat the same day.

title: Kilawing puso ng saging
intro: Thinly sliced banana blossom cooked in vinegar with garlic, ginger and onion, then simmered in coconut milk. It is tangy, creamy and tender, with a texture a bit like artichoke.

steps.text: Peel off the tough, dark outer bracts of the banana blossom until you reach the pale, tender core. Slice it thinly crosswise.
Rub the slices well with the salt and leave until they release their dark sap.
Squeeze the slices hard by the handful, rinse under running water and squeeze dry again.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the garlic, onion and ginger until soft.
Add the banana blossom and the vinegar. Boil without stirring, then stir and cook until the blossom softens.
Pour in the coconut milk and add the chilies. Simmer, stirring now and then, until the sauce thickens slightly. Season with salt and pepper and serve with rice.

tips: Oil your hands or wear gloves when handling banana blossom; the sap stains. Squeeze the slices well, or the dish turns gray and astringent.

title: Kinilaw na bangus
intro: Skinless milkfish belly cut into cubes and cured in vinegar with ginger, onion, chilies and calamansi. The belly is rich and soft, so the sharp dressing tastes especially good with it.

steps.text: Use bangus bought fresh that morning, not frozen boneless packs. Pick out any remaining bones with tweezers and keep the fish cold.
Rinse the cubes in the rinsing vinegar, then drain and discard the vinegar.
Add the curing vinegar, ginger and salt in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl. Refrigerate, tossing once, until the fish is opaque and firm.
Add the calamansi juice, onion, cucumber and chilies. Toss, taste for salt and serve cold.

tips: Bangus belly is fatty, so it can take a slightly longer cure than lean fish without turning dry.

title: Kinilaw na pusit
intro: Squid blanched for a few seconds, sliced into rings and dressed in vinegar with ginger, onion and chilies. It is tender, slightly sweet and sharply sour.

steps.text: Use squid with bright, clear eyes and firm bodies, bought the same day.
Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil and prepare a bowl of ice water. Drop in the squid for 15 seconds, then move it straight into the ice water.
Drain and pat dry. Slice the bodies into thin rings and halve the tentacles.
Toss the squid with the vinegar, calamansi juice, ginger, onion, chilies, salt and pepper in a glass or ceramic bowl.
Refrigerate so the squid soaks up the dressing, then serve cold.

tips: The quick blanch keeps the squid tender and white; any longer and it starts to turn rubbery.

title: Kinilaw na talaba
intro: Freshly shucked oysters in a quick bath of vinegar, calamansi, red onion, ginger and chilies. They are briny, creamy and sharp, and they should be eaten right away.

steps.text: Buy oysters alive from a trusted seller and keep them cold. Discard any with open or cracked shells, or any that smell off.
Shuck the oysters over a bowl to catch their liquor, and put the oysters in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl.
Mix the vinegar, calamansi juice, onion, ginger, chilies and salt, and pour it over the oysters with a few spoonfuls of their liquor.
Let stand in the fridge, then serve at once, spooned back into the shells or in small bowls.

tips: Raw oysters carry more risk than cured fish; skip them for young children, pregnant guests and anyone with a weak immune system. If in doubt, steam the oysters just until they open and dress them the same way.

title: Kilawing labanos
intro: Thin slices of white radish cooked briefly with pork and liver in a garlicky vinegar sauce. The radish stays tender-crisp and soaks up the sour, savory juices.

steps.text: Toss the radish with the salt and leave it to draw out its bitter juice.
Squeeze the radish firmly by the handful, rinse once and squeeze dry.
Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the garlic and onion until soft. Add the pork and cook until lightly browned.
Pour in the vinegar and boil without stirring. Add the water and pepper and simmer until the pork is tender.
Add the liver and cook just until it is no longer pink.
Add the radish and toss until heated through but still a little crisp. Season with salt and serve with rice.

tips: Salting and squeezing the radish takes away its sharp, bitter edge. Do not cook it too long once it goes in, or it turns limp and watery.

title: Kinilaw na lapu-lapu
intro: Fresh grouper cut into cubes and cured in coconut vinegar and lime, then tossed with ginger, shallots, chilies and spring onion. The flesh is sweet and delicate, and the dressing is bright and gingery.

steps.text: Use fish bought the same day and keep it cold in a bowl set over ice while you work.
Put the fish in a chilled glass or ceramic bowl with the vinegar, ginger and salt. Toss gently.
Refrigerate, tossing once, until the cubes are opaque outside and just translucent in the center.
Add the lime juice, shallots, chilies and spring onions. Toss, taste for salt and serve cold right away.

tips: Grouper is delicate, so toss it gently with a spoon rather than stirring hard. Serve within the hour.
